definition: Populism is a political discourse that frames society as divided between a virtuous, homogeneous 'people' and a corrupt, self-serving elite. It claims to represent the true will of the people against an establishment that is out of touch with or hostile to their interests. Populist rhetoric often includes anti-elite sentiment, a people-versus-elite dichotomy, and a call for the people to reclaim power.
inclusion_criteria: A text should be coded as populism if it meets one or more of the following criteria: (1) It explicitly contrasts 'the people' (or similar terms like 'ordinary citizens', 'working families', 'the American people') with a corrupt or self-serving elite (e.g., 'Washington', 'the establishment', 'special interests', 'big corporations', 'politicians'). (2) It accuses the elite of betraying, ignoring, or harming the interests of the people. (3) It positions the speaker as the authentic representative of the people against the elite. (4) It uses anti-establishment rhetoric, such as calling for cleaning out corruption, reclaiming government, or casting out the elite. (5) It frames political issues as a struggle between the common people and a privileged minority. These criteria are not mutually exclusive; typically, multiple criteria are present. A text that only criticizes a specific policy or individual without a systemic critique of elites or a people-versus-elite divide should not be coded as populism.
positive_example: It's going to be a victory for the people. A victory for the everyday citizen whose voice hasn't been heard. It will be a win for the voters – not the pundits, not the journalists, not the lobbyists, not the global special interests funding my opponent's campaign. This meets the criteria by explicitly contrasting 'the people' and 'everyday citizens' with elites (pundits, journalists, lobbyists, special interests) and positioning the speaker as fighting for the people.
negative_example: Just north of where we are gathered tonight passes a historic line that encircles the globe. This line is invisible in America, but in another land it is traced in blood. It is the 38th parallel, the line which divides North and South Korea. This does not meet any criteria; it is a geopolitical observation with no reference to a people-versus-elite divide or anti-elite sentiment.
edge_case_rules: Since there were no cases with confidence below 50%, these rules are based on cases with relatively lower confidence (65-75) to handle ambiguity. (1) If a text highlights the grievances of ordinary people (e.g., mothers, farmers, small businessmen) and implies that these problems are due to systemic neglect or the actions of those in power, it should be coded as populism even if it does not explicitly name an elite. (2) If a text uses anti-elite language but does not clearly contrast the people with a corrupt elite, it may still be populist if it positions the speaker as the people's champion. (3) If a text criticizes a specific policy or individual without a systemic critique of elites or a people-versus-elite divide, it should not be coded as populism. (4) If a text appeals to the people but does not accuse an elite of betraying them, it is likely not populism.
edge_case_example: Mothers know about crowded schools and half-day shifts in many, many places. Farmers know what's happened to prices and costs and their diminishing share of the consumer's food dollar. The small businessman knows what's happened to his credit and his profits. This should be coded as populism because it highlights the grievances of ordinary people and implies that their concerns are overlooked by those in power, even though it does not explicitly name an elite. It appeals to the common people's experience and suggests a systemic problem.
